summary: XPSI Junior Astronaut Training Program is a free browser game that represents a training program played by astronauts, built on actual mission scenarios. Young learners are trainees: they run simulated Moon and Mars missions and keep the base alive. A large live 3D training cam (with a fullscreen toggle) shows colour avatars at work in every annex. Players build their own astronaut and space suit, then share one screen with up to 8 crew. They train through a lunar night power shortfall, a solar particle event shelter drill, an oxygen leak, a crop failure, a comms blackout, a medical emergency drill and a Martian dust storm — each labelled as based on real mission conditions, using real NASA numbers (south-pole sunlight, DONKI storm alerts, Mars and Moon radiation, life-support needs and small fission power). A friendly base Intelligence called VITA guides them, helped by Mobi robots. Kids learn every job, vote for leaders and look after each other. When an area is left alone, plants wilt and the base struggles. A run ends with a training score, skill badges and the line: "The meaning of life is to keep it going." Motto: PSIEE – Preserve. Sustain. Invent. Evolve. Explore.
details:
What it does

The trainer is a representation of an astronaut training program. Young learners play as trainees running simulated missions based on actual scenarios, so they can see and feel the engineering trade-offs of a lunar or Martian outpost. Players run a compact, half-buried base (concept: about 42 m x 41 m, 8 crew and 20 Mobi robots) with a 16 m Nutrodome greenhouse, a Livestock Annex (chickens, goats, fish, pollinator insects), a round Living Module, a Command Pod, a Cargo Pod workshop, an Engineering Pod, a kitchen, and a Smelter Annex reached through a sealed tube. Every section connects to the others and can be sealed off on its own. A large live 3D training cam is the main view of the base, with a fullscreen toggle, and shows colour avatars working in each annex.

How it works

  • Build your crew. Each player designs an astronaut avatar and space suit. Up to 8 players take turns on one device (hot-seat), and the crew is saved in the browser.
  • Prepare. Before the mission, players spend points on stored fuel (ice fuel, recycled-metal fuel), the fleet and cargo deliveries, and complete a first drill: the 50 cm mini engine that still works in a blackout.
  • Run the simulation. A large live 3D training cam, drawn in real time on an HTML canvas, is the main panel on screen and can be opened fullscreen. It shows the base, the crops, the animals, the Mobis and the astronauts walking to their work areas in colour. Players assign crew to each annex, give rest and fun time, and watch the power, battery, oxygen, water, food, shielding and morale gauges.
  • Consequences kids can see. Tired or unhappy astronauts walk out of their work area. Unattended plants wilt and food and oxygen drain faster. When the workshop or Engineering is left unattended, a machine can spark and give a builder a harmless zap (startled, no one hurt).
  • Training scenarios, based on real mission conditions. Each drill is labelled in the game with the NASA (or mission) figures behind it: lunar night power shortfall (LOLA south-pole lighting; dark spells up to about 8 days); solar particle event shelter drill (NASA DONKI, about 20 large events a year); oxygen leak (BVAD: about 0.9 kg O2 per person per day — seal the section); crop failure (closed-loop food and O2; packed food about 2.4 kg/person/day if the garden is down); communications blackout (switch to laser, relays or a Return Ship beacon); medical emergency drill (non-graphic first aid); and a Martian dust storm (several sols; everyday Mars radiation about 0.64 mSv/day vs about 1.37 mSv/day on the Moon). Limited "call the ring station for help" uses add strategy.
  • Levels. Moon (main level): the lunar-night power-shortfall simulation, survived on the battery bunker and fission backup. Mars (level two): regular day and night, a several-sol dust storm, and gentler everyday radiation than the Moon, as NASA measurements show.
  • Community. Basics (air, water, food, clothing) are free for everyone. Kids learn every job and earn skill badges that show ability, not rank. Project leaders are chosen by vote; Mobis flag a leader who stops working for everyone, and the crew can call a recall vote. A crew member who cannot settle can choose to run a refuel out-station, shown as a respectful choice that stays in reach of the base, never a punishment. A wellbeing plan (private quarters, beach and pool, time with animals and plants, calls home, Mobi check-ins) keeps morale up.
  • Ending. A run ends with "Simulation complete" (or "Simulation needs another try"), a training score, skill badges (ability, not rank) and the base's message: "The meaning of life is to keep it going."

Benefits

  • Makes real mission trade-offs tangible and fun without oversimplifying them: power versus food, rest versus work, storing fuel in the sunny season to survive the dark.
  • Uses archived NASA measurements, clearly labelled, so children learn real facts (for example, everyday radiation on the Moon is roughly twice that on the Mars surface).
  • Teaches teamwork, safety drills, fairness, care for animals and mental wellbeing alongside STEM.
  • Free, runs in any modern browser, no install or account, works on one shared classroom screen.
  • Non-graphic and child-safe throughout.

Goals

  • Help young learners experience why outposts succeed or fail.
  • Grow from one base into an underground, glass-lined city dug by the Borer tunnelling machine (future levels), with refuel stations on the routes to Mars and Earth.
  • Add more NASA data hooks (live space-weather and lighting tiles), teacher notes and more languages after the hackathon.

Tools and languages

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with no external libraries.
  • Custom 3D on the HTML5 Canvas 2D API (hand-written projection, shading and day/night sunlight).
  • Browser localStorage for saved crews.
  • Node.js test script (headless browser playtest) for automated checks and screenshots.
  • Hosted as a static web page.

All base figures (17 solar bowls of 10 m on 12 m masts, ~9.8 MWh battery bunker, 2 x 40 kWe fission backup, ~410 kW day / ~160 kW night load) are HeathSilks concept estimates, not NASA measurements.
